Chapter 2: The Subtle Influence of Culture on Faith
Picture this: all across the country, people gather in churches that feel just like their neighborhoods. The buildings are welcoming, the music’s familiar, and the messages lift you up. It’s natural to feel like you belong, like faith just fits right into your everyday routine.
But have you ever wondered if something else is going on beneath the surface? There’s a quiet shift happening—a slow drift where the values of culture start to shape what it means to be a Christian, sometimes without us even noticing.
Imagine a family that’s worked hard for what they have—a nice house in a safe area, kids in good schools, weekends packed with activities. Faith matters to them, but it sits comfortably alongside everything else. They give to charity, volunteer when they can, and show up to church most Sundays. But when they’re asked to step outside their comfort zone—maybe move to a less desirable neighborhood, or give up some personal luxuries to help others—they hesitate. That kind of sacrifice just feels... well, extreme.
And honestly, that’s pretty common. Most of us are shaped by the culture we live in, often without even realizing it. Take the American Dream, for example. It promises that anyone can succeed if they work hard enough. It celebrates independence, self-reliance, and chasing happiness. Over time, these ideas seep into our faith, creating a version of Christianity that’s all about personal comfort and fulfillment.
But if you look at the stories of Jesus, something stands out. He spent time with people on the margins, challenged the wealthy to let go of their possessions, and called his followers to carry their cross. His teachings flipped cultural values upside down. But in so many churches today, those radical words are softened or explained away. Instead of a call to sacrifice, faith becomes a way to improve our lives, find happiness, or tick off our personal goals.
There’s a story about a church leader who realized most of the church’s resources went toward making services more comfortable and appealing—better programs, a welcoming atmosphere, trying to attract more people. But when it came to helping the poor or supporting missions, the enthusiasm just wasn’t there. It hit him: the church was more focused on keeping its members happy than actually living out Jesus’ radical teachings.
And here’s the thing: this kind of shift doesn’t happen overnight. It’s not about bad intentions, but about little choices, made day after day. We all want to feel safe, to enjoy what we’ve worked for. But when comfort is our main goal, faith loses its power to challenge us. Suddenly, following Jesus turns into another path to the “good life,” instead of a call to give everything for others.
So, how do we wake up to the ways culture shapes our faith? It takes more than just showing up at church or believing all the right things. Real discipleship means asking tough questions about the assumptions we’ve inherited, and being ready to let go of comfort and security. It means looking at how we use our time, our money, and our energy—and asking, “What really matters?”
Maybe it’s time to take an honest look at our own lives. Where has culture shaped our faith more than the teachings of Jesus? What if we let go of the American Dream, and embraced a faith that’s truly radical—one that calls us to love boldly, give generously, and step outside our comfort zones?
